To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• The proportion of never-users was higher among the French patients, and heterosexual anal intercourse probably was more widely practised in France.

(1) The proportion of never-users is higher in France and heterosexual anal sex is more widely practised; (2) Approximately 40% (males) and 30% (females) reported more than one partner in the last two years; (3) Patients less than 25 years of age reported more sexual partners and more often used condoms than older patients; (4) There Is no association between condom use in the last six months and perceived risk of HIV-exposure;
(1) The proportion of never-users is lower in France than in Norway.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the sexual behaviour of patients consulting general practitioners, (2) the general practitioners' attitudes towards sexual matters, (3) the general practitioners’ knowledge and skills concerning sexual matters, (4) the general practitioners and their patients' attitudes towards HIV, (5) the general practitioners knowledge about HIV and their skills in HIV counselling and testing, (6) the general practitioners attitudes and skills towards AIDS patients and (7) the general practitioners skills and knowledge about AIDS.

the sexual behaviour of patients attending general practice in France and Norway, with the aim of identifying those who are at risk of HIV infection and who should receive special HIV-related attention in the general practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the French patients have a higher risk for HIV infection than Norwegians, but the differences are not great, that the patients less than 30 year of age are more at risk than patients aged 31 years and older and that there is a need for a more selective approach to HIV-related attention in the general practitioner.
general practitioners in France are less likely than their Norwegian colleagues to be able to direct their attention to the most at risk groups in the HIV epidemic.
general practice in France and Norway is not yet sufficiently HIV selective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
general practitioners should give more selective HIV-related attention, but they should also give it more often.
the HIV-related attention in French general practice is probably more appropriate than in Norwegian general practice.
we need more research on the general practice patients' sexual behaviour, their attitudes to sexuality and to HIV, and their use of general practice services.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that general practitioners can play an important role in the fight against the HIV/AIDS pandemic.
we can't just focus on the most obvious high-risk groups, such as gay men and intravenous drug users, but that the general public is at risk as well.
we need to be careful when we are interpreting the results of our studies.
